Virtual Rubik’s Cube Session Analysis

Project Report for STAT 303-1 Fall 2025

Author

Ben Saperstein

Published

December 9, 2025

Abstract
This project analyzes patterns from a large session of my virtual Rubik’s Cube solutions compiled on cstimer.net. The goals of the analysis were to identify the numeric metrics most associated with improved solve times, measure how my solve times have progressed over time, and identify any trends in solve frequency or solve time associated with temporal variables. The data show that the longest pause in the solution is most strongly associated with the solve time, with a clear positive correlation. Thus, speedcubers should prioritize minimizing hesitations in their solutions as much as possible. My solve times improved rapidly in the initial phases but quickly plateaued, later persisting at a slow and erratic pace. This suggests speedcubers should not be discouraged by periods of stagnation. Solve frequency was lowest on weekends and mornings. Although weekday showed no apparent relationship with solve time, time of day did exhibit a modest effect. The primary limitations of this analysis stem from its reliance on a single individual’s virtual session, inhibiting the scope of the results. The relationships may be nonlinear and it is impossible to infer causality between variables.

1) Inspiration

As a competitive Rubik’s Cube speedsolver, I have always been driven to improve my ability. I took upon this mission at age 11, and I have made incredible progress since. My first ever solution took about 10 minutes with assistance. Now, however, my average time has dropped to about 7.8 seconds, with a record time of 3.72 seconds. My Rubik’s Cube journey has led me to compete in five states for a total of 30 competitions. I am currently ranked 7th fastest in my home state of Michigan, and I hope I can continue to climb the ranks.

In this project, I selected a large sample of my virtual Rubik’s Cube solutions. These solutions were all digitally completed on cstimer.net, where each key on the keyboard corresponds to a different turn or rotation on the Rubik’s Cube. The website tracks and stores a number of variables for each solution, making this project possible. This dataset was compiled over the course of five years, beginning from when I discovered this feature of the website in December 2020.

Through this analysis, I hope to gain valuable information about the factors that are the strongest influences on my solving speed. Perhaps the data may shine a light on what I should emphasize during my solves, contributing to my ultimate goal of a reduction in my average solving time. I would also be curious to see how the variables of each solution changed over time, and see if there are any interesting trends that I was not previously aware of.

2) Problem Statements

Question 1: Which numeric variables appear to have the strongest relationships with solve time? What is the direction and shape of these relationships?

  • I could graph each variable in relation to solve time and generate regression lines to show trends.
  • I could compute the correlation coefficient of each numeric variable with respect to solve time to see which has the strongest link.
  • It is unlikely I will be able to derive a causal link without a controlled experiment.

Question 2: Is there strong evidence of either an improvement or regression in my solve time? What is the shape of the relationship between the solve date and the solve time? Have any other numeric variables undergone significant changes throughout time?

  • I could separate the analysis by including a section of index versus solve time and another section of date versus solve time.
  • I could create scatterplots with regression lines and barplots with error bars to visualize the relationships.
  • I could also display dataframes with the corresponding raw numerical data.

Question 3: What are the trends related to the temporal data of each solution? What are the most and least common days of the week and times of the day for me to complete virtual solutions? Are solve times influenced by the the day of the week or the time of day?

  • I could generate visualizations to see if there are differences in solve frequency between the days of the week and the times of day.
  • I could create a heatmap that displays the solve frequency according to both the day of the week and the time of day.
  • I could graph the mean solve time for each combination of the day of the week and the time of day.

3) Data

I exported my session data from cstimer.net using the embedded “export to file” feature in the website. The file was 25 MB in size, and consisted of all my sessions. I needed to narrow down the data to only my virtual Rubik’s Cube solutions, so I only extracted “session36” from the .txt file. Since the raw data file is extremely large and contains many unrelated sessions, I am unable to include it in this submission.

Given the complexity and nested structure of the exported data, with the permission of Professor Behera, I used AI to write code in order to cleanly store my relevant session data in a Pandas dataframe. I instructed it to write several functions to compute values that are not directly apparent from the exported data, but are useful to my analysis.

After processing and cleaning, there are a total of 16,776 observations and 14 variables in the dataframe. Each observation represents the completion of a Rubik’s Cube solution. Of the 14 variables, nine are numeric and five are categorical.

Numeric Variables

  1. “solve_time_s” - The amount of time (in seconds) taken to return the Rubik’s Cube to a solved state
  2. “number_of_turns” - The number of times a side of the Rubik’s Cube was turned
  3. “turn_speed_tps” - The number of turns completed every second (e.g. “number_of_turns” / “solve_time_s”)
  4. “number_of_rotations” - The number of times the user flips the cube to view another angle
  5. “total_move_count” - A sum of the number of turns and the number of rotations (total keyboard clicks)
  6. “longest_pause_ms” - The greatest gap in time between two consecutive moves
  7. “fastest_burst_10_moves_ms” - The shortest time period in which ten consecutive turns take place
  8. “wasted_moves” - The number of times a move is immediately followed by its inverse, thereby leaving the state of the cube unchanged
  9. “scramble_length” - The number of turns specified in the computer-generated scramble

Categorical Variables

  1. “date” - The date of the solution provided in (YYYY-MM-DD) format
  2. “day_of_week” - The day of week of the solution
  3. “time” - The time of day of the solution given in military time
  4. “time_of_day_bucket” - One of four labels based on the time of day of the solution (Late Night, Morning, Afternoon, Evening)
  5. “scramble” - The computer-generated sequence of turns, expressed in speedcubing notation, that reaches the cube’s initial state

The numeric variables will be used to address primarily Question 1, while the categorical variables are uniquely helpful to shed insight on Question 3. Both a numerical and categorical variable (“solve_time_s” and “date” respectively) are critical for Question 2.

4) Stakeholders

The primary stakeholder of this project is myself. Not only am I inherently interested in discovering any trends in my data, but also this may have a notable impact on the strategies I used to improve my solve time moving forward. Based on the conclusions of this analysis, I may shift focus during my practice sessions to better address the factors that most greatly affect the speed of the solution. Perhaps I will emphasize increasing my turning speed, prioritizing efficiency, limiting rotations, reducing pauses, or make adjustments with a number of other contributing variables.

As I chase my first sub-8 second average in competition, any improvement whatsoever could play a major role in my results.

In addition, secondary stakeholders include the entire Rubik’s Cube speedsolving community. Other speedsolvers will surely be interested in seeing the relationships I discover, as it may help them with their own progression journeys. I look forward to sharing the conclusions of this project with the members of the Northwestern Cubing Club and the other competitors at my Rubik’s Cube tournaments.

5) Data Cleaning

Data Cleaning Applicable to all Questions

Missing Values

By nature of the dataset, there are no missing values. There have been occasions throughout the past five years where I have hit the “esc” key before finishing the solution. These solves are marked as “DNF”, which is an acronym for did not finish. These rows would create NaN values in columns such as “solve_time_s” and would hence need to be deleted from the dataframe. Luckily, however, I always delete those solutions from the session so that these DNFs would not interfere with my rolling averages. In a way, I have already manually cleaned the data through its entire existence.

Valid Function Output

It would be possible for there to be NaNs based on some of the functions used to calculate certain numeric variables. For instance, the column “fastest_burst_10_moves_ms” requires the solution to be at least 10 moves in length. However, given that the minimum “number_of_turns” value is 38 for the session, this issue never arose. Hence, all the columns that are the output of a function contain non-null, appropriate results.

Useless Category

One category, “scramble”, is essentially useless to this analysis. The “scramble” column contains the turns, shown in Rubik’s Cube notation, required to reach the computer-generated initial state for that particular row. Given that the “scramble” appears in Rubik’s Cube notation, this category by itself cannot be used to parse any meaningful data. While the scramble is unlikely to yield any significant conclusions in the analysis, it may be helpful when reconstructing solutions manually and hence it would be unwise to discard that information.

a) Cleaning - Question 1

Though all the rows contain valid values, some of them may not be fully representative of my solving ability. Hence, for the purpose of determining which numeric variables have the strongest relationship with solve time, certain rows should be treated as outliers and hence excluded from the analysis.

Handling Outliers: Longest Pause

One such category with outliers is “longest_pause_ms”. There may be rows that represent solutions in which I was distracted or took a quick break during the solution. Typically, outliers can be found using Tukey’s fences. However, Tukey’s fences are designed to find outliers in roughly symmetric data. In this case, the first few hundred rows create a skew that leads to Tukey’s fences identifying 896 outliers.

Instead of taking the Tukey’s fences approach to deal with outliers for “longest_pause_ms”, a uniform comparison is superior. At my level of Rubik’s Cube ability, where I often plan more than 10 moves ahead at any given moment, we can reasonably assume that a pause of greater than 3 seconds (or 3000 milliseconds) is not a genuine attempt at the fastest possible solution. Instead, it is safer to conclude there was some confounding variable. This comes with the caveat that earlier rows may naturally have longer pauses because I was still learning the controls of the virtual Rubik’s Cube. These are valuable rows to the analysis and thus the pauses should not be treated as outliers. In the dataset, there are 63 rows in which “longest_pause_ms” is greater than 3000, but only 12 such rows where the index > 500. These rows can be excluded for the purpose of the analysis.

Handling Outliers: Number of Rotations

Similarly, another category with outliers that corrupt the dataset is “number_of_rotations”. A cube rotation is not a turn of one of the sides, but rather a change in the angle in which the user is facing while viewing the virtual cube. With a physical Rubik’s Cube, I tend to average about three rotations per solution. For ergonomic reasons, there is a greater incentive to rotate with a virtual cube than with a physical cube. Hence, the mean value for “number_of_rotations” in the virtual session is about 11. That being said, there are rows that contain many more rotations. For the purpose of identifying outliers, I will assume that any solution with over 25 rotations does not reflect a genuine attempt at the fastest possible solution. 25 rotations is much higher than the mean, and these rows may be better explained by confounding variables such as me experimenting with new algorithms, doing several rotations subsequently out of boredom, or demonstrating my thought process during a solution to a friend. And using the same logic as before, earlier rows should not be excluded since I was still adapting to the controls. The dataframe contains 109 rows in which “number_of_rotations” is greater than 25, but only 68 such rows where the index > 500.

With the aforementioned standards, there are 12 outliers for “longest_pause_ms” and 68 outliers for “number_of_rotations”. After filtering the data to eliminate these outliers, the number of rows is reduced from 16856 to 16776. This indicates that there was no overlap between the outliers for these two categories. With the outliers eliminated, the analysis is better suited to uncover which variables truly correlate most strongly with solve time.

b) Cleaning - Question 2

No further data cleaning is required for this problem statement. Each row contains a valid index, date, and solve time. The outliers discussed in Question 1 are eliminated by this point, so every remaining row should contain a solution that contains accurate and valid data.

d) Cleaning - Question 3

The process of cleaning the raw timestamp data was already completed during the processing and creation of the dataframe. Using the timestamp, three new columns were created using .dt.date, .dt.time, and dt.day_name().

Sorting Time of Day into Buckets

It would be difficult to perform data analysis techniques on the time of day alone since it is a cyclical, continuous numerical variable, so the times of day for each row were sorted into four categorical buckets: Late Night (12:00 AM - 5:59 AM), Morning (6:00 AM - 11:59 AM), Afternoon (12:00 PM - 5:59 PM), and Evening (6:00 PM - 11:59 PM). Each bucket has a duration of 6 hours. By processing the times of day into buckets, it is easier to identify temporal trends with respect to solve frequency and solve time.

6) Data Analysis

a) Analysis 1

Question 1: Which numeric variables appear to have the strongest relationships with solve time? What is the direction and shape of these relationships?

6.1.1: Approach

The goal of this section is to determine which numeric variables in the dataset are most strongly related to solve time. There are eight numeric variables excluding solve time that must be taken into account. Some are continuous, such as “turn_speed_tps” and “longest_pause_ms”, while others are discrete, such as “number_of_turns” and “wasted_moves”. Regardless, these continuous and discrete variables can be treated indiscriminately throughout the analysis.

Though I would like to perform regressions and obtain data such as the 95% confidence interval for the slope of the fitted line, that is beyond the scope of this project report, as these concepts will be explored in the second quarter of the course. Instead, we will use graphs and correlation coefficients to identify trends in the data.

6.1.2: Scatterplot

My first instinct was to create scatterplots with regression lines to visualize the relationship between each variable and solve time. There are eight graphs total, with solve time remaining on the y-axis throughout. For the sake of better identifying trends, the y-axis is set to extend to a maximum of 30 seconds. Though many earlier rows contain solve times of greater than 30 seconds, the vast majority of the data is contained in the 6-20 second range.

Shown below are the scatterplots for each numeric variable plotted against solve time.

The scatterplots help reveal the direction of the relationships. Turn speed and solve time appear to have a negative relationship. Scramble length and solve time have a vaguely positive relationship, although it is unclear if this trend is significantly significant. All other numeric variables have a positive relationship with solve time.

However, given the clustered nature of the data, it is difficult to make any conclusions on the strengths or shapes of these relationships. As a result, we need to visualize the data with another approach that could display these trends more elegantly.

6.1.3: Barplot

Using a barplot instead, we can group the x-variable into bins. We can then effectively plot the bins against the mean solve time for those data points. Given the size of the dataset, the bins will be created with equal length, but not necessarily equal size. The majority of bins are likely to contain a sufficient amount of data such that we avoid problems with high variance. The error bars are shown to demonstrate the confidence for each mean solve time.

To avoid extreme cases having an overly dominant impact, the visualization is performed on a dataset that excludes the first 300 entries. This is done to protect the scaling of the figure so that the relationships for the remaining 16,000+ data points can be identified.

Shown below are the barplots for each variable plotted against mean solve time.

Similar to the scatterplots, the barplots show the direction of the relationships. More importantly, however, they illustrate the shapes and confidence levels of these relationships. Many of the relationships appear to be roughly linear, whether it is positive or negative in direction. There appears to be no link between scramble length and solve time, though the first bin has a much higher mean solve time than the rest. At the same time, it has a relatively large error bar, so it is difficult to draw conclusions solely based on that bin.

Though the shapes are much more apparent in this visualization, the strengths of these relationships are still unclear.

6.1.4: Correlation Barplot

To test the strength of the relationship between each variable and solve time, we can calculate the correlation coefficients. We can sort the numeric variables based on the correlation coefficients they share with solve time and visualize these with a barplot. Since the directions of these relationships are irrelevant to their strengths, it is best to take the absolute value of each correlation coefficient during a visualization.

Shown below are the absolute correlations between each variable and solve time.

The two variables that have the strongest relationships with solve time include “longest_pause_ms” and “fastest_burst_10_moves_ms”, with correlations of approximately 0.695 and 0.673 respectively. On the other hand, the variable with unmistakably the weakest relationship with solve time is “scramble_length”, which has a correlation of approximately 0.008.

6.1.5: Answer

Based on the graphs and figures from 6.1.2-6.1.4, the numeric variable that shares the strongest relationship with solve time is the length of the longest pause, though the fastest burst of 10 moves is very close.

The relationship between the longest pause and solve time is positive and roughly linear. As the longest pause increases in duration, so does the solve time.

Most speedcubers would expect their turn speed or efficiency (which is proxied by number of turns) to have the greatest impact on their solve times. Since solve time can be expressed as number of turns divided by turn speed, both variables undoubtedly contribute greatly towards faster solutions. However, there is an important tradeoff to be considered. As turn speed increases for a solver, their efficiency tends to suffer. Likewise, more efficient solutions contribute towards slower turn speeds. For that reason, improving in one metric would not necessarily guarantee faster solve times.

However, pausing during a solution is directly harmful to the solve time. Any time spent without making turns is simply time that gets added to the clock without progressing any further. The fact that the longest pause is the variable that correlates most strongly with solve time would not be terribly surprising to the speedcubing community.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, scramble length has almost no relationship with solve time. A 14 move scramble is not inherently better than a 21 move scramble for human solvers. A robot that computes the move optimal solution ahead of time would benefit from shorter scrambles, but humans cannot identify the optimal route after the cube is more than a couple moves away from the solved state. There is no distinct visual difference in the random initial states between shorter scrambles compared to longer scrambles, so they are practically the same for human solvers who impose their own methods on the puzzle.

b) Analysis 2

Question 2: Is there strong evidence of either an improvement or regression in my solve time? What is the shape of the relationship between the solve date and the solve time? Have any other numeric variables undergone significant changes throughout time?

6.2.1: Approach

In this analysis, I will evaluate how my solve time has changed over time, both in direction and shape. While solve time will be the dependent variable, there are two options for the independent variable: index and date. The index will signify how my solves improve sequentially, while the date shows the rate of improvement over time. Both approaches have unique strengths and weaknesses. Working with only the index will only show how much I improve as a result of completing more solutions. This is excellent for showing learning progression because it tracks my improvement as experience accumulates. On the other hand, performing analysis on the date will show my progression over time irrespective of how much I devote to practicing. This will provide useful statistics such as my monthly and annual rate of improvement.

Though I would like to perform regressions to generate nonlinear models and compare the residual sum of squares between the model specifications, that is outside the scope of the course. Instead, I will use graphs and charts to visualize the data, where the shape of the relationship can be inferred visually.

6.2.2: Index vs Solve Time Scatterplot

The first visualization will be a scatterplot with a fitted regression line superimposed. The regression line will help show the strength of the relationship. To account for improvement with the earlier solutions, the maximum y-value is set to 60 seconds.

Shown below is the scatterplot that shows the relationship between solve index and solve time.

The data show a steep, negative trend for the earlier data points. This is during the time when I was getting used to the controls of the virtual Rubik’s Cube. The regression line is modestly negative for the entire dataset, though it is unclear if a systematic decrease in solve time persisted after the first few thousand solves. To differentiate between the clustered data points in the later solves indices, a different visualization will be more useful.

6.2.3: Index vs Solve Time Barplot

Just like in 6.1.2, we can group the indices into bins. In our case, the bin size is set to 500 to create a total of 34 bins. All the bins have 500 data points except for the final one, which contains 276 data points. From there, we compute the mean solve time for each bin. Each bar is connected by a red line to show how solve time increases or decreases as the solve index rises.

Shown below is the barplot that visualizes the relationship between the index range to the mean solve time. A dataframe is also displayed to show the raw values for each mean solve time.

6.2.4: Date vs Solve Time Scatterplot

This visualization is largely similar to that shown in 6.1.2, but with date as the regressor instead of index. The model includes a fitted regression line as well. The entries from December of 2020 are removed for this model and that of 6.2.5-6.2.6 because the sample size is very limited and these data points are outliers in terms of solve date.

Shown below is the scatterplot that compares date to mean solve time.

As expected, the data shown in this visualization are similar to that seen in 6.1.2 with the scatterplot of indices. A modest downward trend is apparent by the fitted regression line. The graph contains many more missing sections since the data is sorted temporally. There are several months from March 2023 onward that do not contain any entries in the dataset.

In alignment with the other scatterplots, it is difficult to identify whether there was any systematic decrease in solve time after the first few months. The downward tilt in the regression line could simply be attributed to the higher solve times for the first few thousand entries. Even if the remainder of the data has comparable solve times to each other, the regression line would be biased downward.

6.2.6: Change over Time for Other Numeric Variables

While solve time is the most important numeric variable for this analysis, it is possible that other eight numeric variables have also changed over time.

Shown below are eight barplots that compare month to each numeric variable.

For many of the graphs, March 2023 is vastly different since I was still learning the controls of the virtual Rubik’s Cube. Some numeric variables remain relatively consistent, such as number of turns, while others demonstrate slow progression, such as turn speed. The fact that some variables are essentially equal throughout makes sense given that I was already a seasoned speedcuber when learning the virtual Rubik’s Cube. My solving method has been the same since before 2023, so I would not expect a statistically significant progression. However, variables like turn speed has improved because that is heavily tied to my comfort level of navigating the keyboard controls for the virtual Rubik’s Cube.

As a whole, the other numeric variables appear much steadier over time in comparison to solve time.

6.2.7: Answer

Based on the graphs and numeric data, there is a clear systematic improvement in my solve time. This can be seen whether using index or date as the independent variable. The rate of progression was rapid at first, but then became slow and erratic after the initial phases. Though there are reversions on occasion, the visualizations and dataframes demonstrate that the general trend is towards lower solve times. This trend persists even in the later months in the dataset.

Many numeric variables seem unchanged as time passes, such as number of turns and scramble length, while others exhibit minor improvements over time, such as turn speed and fastest burst of 10 moves.

c) Analysis 3

Question 3: What are the trends related to the temporal data of each solution? What are the most and least common days of the week and times of the day for me to complete virtual solutions? Are solve times influenced by the the day of the week or the time of day?

6.3.1: Approach

In this section, we will focus exclusively on the day of week and time of day bucket as our temporal variables. These are categorical, with seven and four categories respectively. This eases the process of analysis since .groupby is available. The analysis will take into account both the frequency of solves and the mean solve time for every unique combination of day of week and time of day.

6.3.2: Frequency of Virtual Solves by Day of Week

We will start by graphing the absolute frequencies of each day of the week in the dataset.

Shown below is the barplot.

day_of_week count

The graph and dataframe signify that the most common days for me to practice virtual Rubik’s Cube solves are Monday and Tuesday, while the least common are Saturday and Sunday.

I tend to use the virtual Rubik’s Cube as a substitute to a physical Rubik’s Cube when I am in a quiet setting, like in lecture or at the library. The virtual cube is much less disruptive, so I spend time solving it primarily as a study break. Mondays and Tuesdays are the days where I spend the most time in quiet settings.

On Saturdays and Sundays, I may spend more time away from technology, which means less virtual Rubik’s Cube solutions. Furthermore, I am more frequently in my dorm room on weekends, so I would have access to a physical Rubik’s Cube, and those solutions are not encompassed by this dataset.

6.3.3: Frequency of Virtual Solves by Time of Day

We will continue the exploration by graphing the absolute frequencies of each time of day category in the dataset.

Shown below is the barplot.

time_of_day_bucket count

The graph and dataframe signify that the most common time of day for me to practice virtual Rubik’s Cube solves is the evening (6:00 PM - 11:59 PM), while the least common is the morning (6:00 AM - 11:59 AM).

Carrying over the logic from 6.3.2, since I primarily use the virtual Rubik’s Cube as a study break in a quiet setting, I would expect the most frequent time of day to be the evening. Most of the time I am working at the library, it is indeed between 6:00 PM and 11:59 PM. The data thus align with my prediction.

By the same token, it is also sensible that the morning is the least frequent time of day bucket. Most days, I wake up at around 10:00 AM. Hence, I am asleep for the majority of the morning bucket. Once I wake up, I am still unlikely to solve the virtual Rubik’s Cube. Instead, I tend to be getting ready for the day, eating breakfast, and preparing for class. The fact that morning is the least frequent bucket by a significant margin is therefore expected.

6.3.4: Heatmap of Solve Counts by Day of Week and Time of Day

Though it is useful to view the day of week and time of day separately beforehand, there may be interesting correlations between the two categorical variables. Thus, a visualization that displays solve frequency based on both may prove useful.

Shown below is a heatmap of solve counts based on time of day and day of week.

Though the trends with day of week and time of day from 6.3.2-6.3.3 can be visualized with this heatmap as well, some other interesting trends arise. For instance, Saturday and Sunday are fundamentally similar for most of the time of day buckets. However, Sunday evening has more than three times the solve counts than Saturday evening has. One possible explanation is that I may be at the library on Sunday evenings to work on some of the weekend assignments I had procrastinated. And, of course, I would have used the virtual Rubik’s Cube as my study break.

Sunday morning is the least common, while Tuesday evening is the most common. The variance between the entries in the graph seem to be affected more greatly by time of day than they are by day of week.

6.3.5: Heatmap of Mean Solve Time by Day of Week and Time of Day

Using a similar heatmap from 6.3.4, we can display mean solve time instead of solve count. This will show if there is any measurable impact on my solving speed based on the day of week or time of day.

Shown below is a heatmap of mean solve time based on time of day and day of week.

A number of notable relationships are shown by the heatmap.

For one, Wednesday evening has the highest mean solve time for a large margin. Given the large sample size, this seems improbable. Upon further analysis, however, it is apparent that the Wednesday evening bucket was skewed by a disproportionate number of earlier entries. I began practicing the virtual Rubik’s Cube again for the first time in over two years at 6:24 PM on March 22, 2023. This was, unsurprisingly, a Wednesday. Solve indices 16-84 all occurred on this Wednesday evening, and of these 69 solves, there was a mean solve time of 53.98 seconds. This is nearly 10% percent of all solves that have taken place on all Wednesday evenings, which is enough to create a large upward bias in the data.

There does not appear to be a significant relationship between day of week and mean solve time. However, time of day may have a consequential impact. Late night has only one mean of under 13 seconds and afternoon does not have any. On the other hand, morning has five means under 13 seconds and evening has four means under 13 seconds. Given the large sample size, there may be a real-world correlation. Solving late at night would undermine my performance, so I expect my solve times to be slightly higher. The afternoon is not as easy to explain, but it could be because I tend to do virtual Rubik’s Cube solves before lecture and during pauses, so I am not as fully focused as I would be in other settings.

Without confidence intervals, though, it is difficult to make conclusions with any degree of certainty. The variations may be expected based on the sample size and confounding variables.

6.3.6: Answer

The individual results are summarized in each section of 6.3. As a whole, both day of week and time of day do have a significant impact on solve frequency. When the two categorical variables are combined to generate 28 categories, there are some combinations between specific days of the week and times of the day that are more or less common than one would expect by looking at the day of week and time of day data separately. Furthermore, there seems to be a link between time of day and mean solve time, but no such relationship is apparent in the visualizations between day of week and mean solve time.

7) Recommendations to Stakeholders

a) Recommendations 1

Based on the analysis, in order to continue decreasing my solve time, I should prioritize limiting pauses during my solutions. Since the length of the longest pause is correlated most strongly with solve time, I should take measures to reduce pausing as much as possible. Reducing pauses is much easier said than done, but there are steps I can take. I can plan further ahead into my solution during inspection time to eliminate the pause after forming the white cross. Another improvement would be to practice fluid, consistent turning rather than turning in bursts. Finally, I can memorize how a variety of pieces are affected after the execution of an algorithm to better predict the state of the cube several moves in advance. Other members of the speedcubing community can implement the same principles to their practice regimen in order to reduce their solve times.

One crucial limitation of this analysis is the medium of every solution in the dataset. All solutions were completely virtually on cstimer.net, but I care much more about my solving ability with a physical Rubik’s Cube. Officially sanctioned competitions only include physical Rubik’s Cube events, so if I want to climb the rankings, I would like to analyze data that can translate over to non-virtual solutions.

Though there is significant overlap between the physical and virtual Rubik’s Cube, there are just as many key distinctions. For instance, the virtual cube is much harder to view since the computer presents an angle that shows only the front and top faces, but a solver can see three faces at a time on a physical cube. Most importantly, though, the virtual Rubik’s Cube has no regard for turning ergonomics. Half the battle on a Rubik’s Cube is not what turns the solver is doing, but how they are doing them. I spend a lot of time optimizing my solving style to minimize regripping and overworking a finger. For instance, I may complete a turn of the top face by completing a left index drag rather than a right thumb and index pinch, and this all depends on the previous positions of my hands as well as where I would like them to be at the beginning of the next sequence of moves. The virtual cube, on the other hand, is strictly completed through a keyboard.

The only way to fully overcome these limitations is by using a sample of physical Rubik’s Cube solutions instead. The virtual cube is remarkably convenient because it stores each move as well as the corresponding timestamp, down to the millisecond. In order to do the same with a physical Rubik’s Cube, a solver would need to use a “smart” cube. These contain internal sensors that track the moves and connect to an app via Bluetooth. Unfortunately, these cubes also tend to be heavy and suboptimal for speedcubing. A speedcuber could also conduct a manual frame-by-frame analysis on each of their solutions, but that would be immensely laborious.

Rather than overcoming the disconnect between virtual and physical solutions, it is best to recognize the limited scope of the analysis. There are enough commonalities that general trends and insights will remain the same, but the virtual Rubik’s Cube can not be used as a perfect proxy for physical Rubik’s Cube speedsolving.

b) Recommendations 2

The results from the analysis outlined in 6.2.1-6.2.7 mirror the traditional learning curve for any subject. Progression appears to be abundant in earlier stages, but improvement grows slower and more irregular as time passes. For the stakeholders, being myself and other speedcubers, these findings can help encourage us when it seems like there is no improvement. A speedcuber may incorrectly feel that their times are not trending downwards, when in fact, they are. Although an intermediate speedcuber may be dissatisfied that their times are not dropping like they used to, that does not mean that improvement has faded entirely. It is entirely possible that their progression has just slowed and grew in irregularity. With that being said, this analysis should not be a justification for being complacent with their practice regimen. All speedcubers who are seeking to improve their times should take the necessary measures to boost their speed, including drilling their algorithms and working on their look ahead during the first two layers.

The major limitation in this analysis is the statistical resources I was permitted to access. We were told to save inference analysis and advanced regression techniques for the future iteration of this project report. Thus, I only used linear regressions. It is reasonable, and in fact likely, that my data would be better explained by a power or an exponential model. Also, I did not have the resources to determine the error for our estimator of the slope of improvement. Using the standard error of the slope estimator would allow us to draw conclusions about whether the slope estimate is significantly different from 0 under different significance levels. It would also allow us to create a confidence interval for the true value of the slope. Overall, these extra statistical tools would better explain my data and provide us the resources to make more powerful and accurate conclusions.

c) Recommendations 3

The visualizations in 6.3.2-6.3.4 are simply a function of solve frequency, which is something I as a stakeholder was curious about. However, this insight will not necessarily help me improve my solve times. The visualization in 6.3.5, on the other hand, revealed a relationship between time of day and solve time. I tend to solve faster in the mornings and evenings than afternoons and late nights. If I would like to drop my average, perhaps I could make a conscious effort to complete more virtual cube practice sessions in the morning and evening, and avoid afternoons and late nights. In general, I should be sharper and more focused during those sessions than I currently am during the average virtual cube solution. Though this is a dataset of my solutions, other speedcubers may consider these findings useful. Perhaps they could structure their day to include practice sessions exclusively in the morning and evening as well. The scope of the data may be limited, as the speedcubers would have to be sufficiently similar to me in order for these results to translate to their own times.

Another crucial limitation is the lack of causality. It is unclear whether the time of day causes my solve times to increase or decrease. It could be a correlation that is generated by confounding variables not included in the analysis. In order to develop a clear causal link, I would need to conduct an experiment with an adequately large sample size in which I complete a predetermined number of solutions at specified time intervals throughout the day. All other variables such as environment would have to be held constant to suggest a causal relationship.

8) Conclusion

Taken together, the analyses reveal a holistic understanding of my speedcubing performance that cannot be achieved with one question alone. A number of variables contribute to every solution I complete, whether it is my control or not. As a speedcuber on a mission to progress as much as possible, I need to be more intentional in scheduling my practice sessions, focusing on the most high impact aspects of my solutions, and continuing to further push the boundaries of what I believed to be possible for myself by shaving off more and more milliseconds.

No one metric alone will ever encompass my speedcubing performance. I heard a speedcuber offer an analogy before, and I believe sharing it would be pertinent. A speedcuber can be compared to a ship at sea. When they first start off, the ship is riddled with holes which lead to it beginning to sink. We are only humans, so we can only patch one hole at a time. For a speedcuber, they may “patch their hole” by learning a new algorithm or discovering another angle to recognize a pattern. Everyone begins with a number of weaknesses. However, after they patch their holes enough times, one might realize that their ship is staying afloat quite well. There are too many facets of speedcubing to focus on at any one moment, but in the long run, progression does happen when the weakest areas are targeted and eliminated.

This concept of speedcubing progression extends far beyond the edges of the 3x3x3 puzzle. Being deliberate with practice sessions, addressing weaknesses, and persisting even when results are not readily apparent are all skills that are applicable to any field of human endeavor. Moving forward, I hope that myself and others can internalize these lessons and incorporate them into many other aspects of life.

  1. Click on “option” with the gear icon in the top left corner of the screen.
